extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and media scholars researching journalism history and media practices
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the characteristic features and practices historically associated with 'yellow journalism' (the sensationalist press style of the late 19th/early 20th century) and how those practices functioned to drive circulation and influence public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalistic/exaggerated headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of eye-catching headlines and sensationalized exaggerations for increased sales; "scare headlines in huge print, often sensationalizing minor news."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include large multi-column front-page headlines and hyperbolic copy (e.g., the San Francisco Examiner's melodramatic hotel fire headline). Function: arrest attention and drive street-vendor sales. Anti-pattern: misleading headline that overstates or distorts the underlying facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lavish use of pictures, illustrations, and color
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent and prominent use of illustrations, imaginary drawings, and often full-color pages to attract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes emphasis on full-color Sunday supplements and the use of comic strips (notably the Yellow Kid) as a circulation driver. Publishers invested in bold layouts, large illustrations, and color to make papers more entertaining and marketable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavy reliance on unnamed sources and unverified claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of unverified claims and a heavy reliance on unnamed sources rather than fully corroborated reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism historian W. Joseph Campbell highlighted dependence on unnamed sources as a yellow-press trait. This practice increases speed and sensational appeal at the cost of reliability; it's an anti-pattern for rigorous journalism and a common cause of factual errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faked interviews, misleading headlines, pseudoscience, and false experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of fabricated interviews, misleading headlines, promotion of pseudoscientific claims, and use of so-called experts to lend false authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frank Luther Mott identified this pattern: faked interviews and a 'parade of false learning from so-called experts.' Such practices manufacture authority and narrative where evidence is weak or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on sensationalized crime and scandal reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritizing crime, scandal, adultery, and violence in coverage to excite public interest and boost sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Examiner devoted large percentages of space to crime, presenting stories as morality plays. This emphasis can distort news judgment by elevating lurid or marginal incidents above matters of greater public importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-promotion and unabashed marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Active self-promotion of the newspaper (and its framing of events) as part of editorial strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campbell notes 'unabashed self-promotion' as characteristic of the yellow press. Tactics included front-page bragging, contests, stunts, and direct appeals to readers. This blends editorial voice with commercial marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comic supplements and popular features to drive mass appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Featuring comic strips and lightweight entertainment (e.g., the Yellow Kid) prominently to attract a large readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunday entertainment features and comic-strip pages functioned like weekly magazines; the Yellow Kid strip was central to the coining and identity of 'yellow journalism.' This editorial mix favored entertainment value over depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic sympathy with the 'underdog' and populist framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraying clear sympathy for the 'underdog' and positioning stories as fights against the system to enlist reader emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mott listed 'dramatic sympathy with the "underdog" against the system' as a trait. While populist framing can mobilize readers, in yellow journalism it often served to sensationalize and simplify complex issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bold layout and multi-topic front pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily multi-column front-page headlines covering a variety of topics (sports, scandal, etc.) with bold layouts designed to attract attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campbell's description emphasizes front-page variety and layout as a design strategy: large headlines, many columns, and bold visuals. The approach prioritizes visual impact and breadth of sensational topics on the front page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial circulation tactics (price-cutting, stunts, staff raids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Business strategies used to grow circulation, such as cutting the paper price to a penny, organizing stunts/contests, and raiding rival staffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Hearst kept the Journal at one cent and ran contests and stunts; he also lured journalists from rivals. These tactics show how commercial imperatives shaped editorial choices toward sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing crusades/social reform with sensational methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining sensationalism and entertainment with crusades against corruption and public-interest reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pulitzer used sensational techniques but also pursued social reform journalism. This nuance shows yellow papers could include serious reporting; criterion: sensational form coupled with advocacy or crusading content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing or exaggerating events to influence public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggerating, dramatizing, or allegedly manufacturing aspects of events to inflame readers and shape public sentiment (e.g., alleged role in Spanish–American War coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page discusses debates over whether yellow journalism pushed the U.S. into war; regardless, the practice of amplifying or embellishing events to provoke emotional response is a defining evaluative criterion and an ethical concern.
